metadata.summary: Translate nutrition, activity, alcohol counseling, and appropriate weight management into a supported plan with measurable goals and follow-up.
concepts: Alcohol abstinence with F2 or greater
metadata.application: Agree on a feasible nutrition change and activity schedule, document the outcome being targeted, arrange support, and set a reassessment date.
keyPoints: Modest weight loss can improve steatosis; fibrosis improvement generally requires greater loss.
Activity can benefit the liver without weight loss.
Clinically significant fibrosis warrants complete alcohol abstinence.
Tailor the plan to nutrition, function, access, and preferences.

bodies.heading: Match weight loss to outcome
bodies.body: For an adult with overweight or obesity, an individualized calorie deficit can support weight reduction. AASLD describes 3-5% weight loss as improving steatosis, while greater sustained loss, generally above 10%, is needed to improve steatohepatitis and fibrosis. These are outcome-specific associations, not guaranteed responses or proof that a particular patient’s scar has resolved. A lean patient can benefit from diet quality and activity without automatically needing weight loss.

bodies.heading: Work the percentage correctly
bodies.body: Weight loss (%) = (starting weight - current weight) / starting weight × 100. A change from 100 kg to 96 kg is 4%: (100 - 96) / 100 × 100 = 4. This fits the modest-loss range associated with steatosis improvement; it does not demonstrate MASH resolution or fibrosis regression. Keep the same units and starting-weight denominator when following the trend.

bodies.heading: Build the eating pattern
bodies.body: Favor fiber-rich vegetables, legumes, whole grains, and unsaturated fats while reducing excess saturated fat, refined carbohydrates, and sugar-sweetened beverages. A Mediterranean-style pattern has cardiovascular benefits and can reduce liver fat, but superiority over every other sustainable dietary approach is not established. Adapt food choices to culture, preferences, affordability, and nutritional needs rather than prescribing one universal restrictive diet.

bodies.heading: Prescribe activity
bodies.body: Physical activity has liver and cardiometabolic benefits independent of weight loss. Tailor aerobic and resistance activity to the patient’s abilities and preferences. A practical moderate aerobic target is at least 150 minutes per week when feasible; five 30-minute sessions total 150 minutes. Start from current function and progress safely. A stable scale weight or normal ALT is not a reason to defer activity.

bodies.heading: Address alcohol explicitly
bodies.body: Reassess the amount and pattern of alcohol use over time. Alcohol can contribute to liver disease progression, and a nomenclature boundary is not a safe-drinking limit. AASLD recommends complete abstinence for clinically significant fibrosis, F2 or greater. A general diabetes recommendation to avoid or moderate alcohol must not override this fibrosis-specific advice.

bodies.heading: Design maintenance
bodies.body: Arrange continuing dietitian and behavioral support, assess social and psychological barriers, and schedule follow-up. Review weight trajectory, activity, diet, metabolic measures, and liver-risk assessment in context. Consider anti-obesity pharmacotherapy or metabolic surgery assessment when indicated; these support sustained treatment rather than replace nutrition and activity. Discuss sleep symptoms and connect suspected sleep apnea with appropriate evaluation.

bodies.heading: Respect nutrition and cirrhosis boundaries
bodies.body: Metabolic surgery can benefit eligible patients without cirrhosis, but eligibility and procedure selection require an individualized assessment. Compensated cirrhosis calls for expert benefit-risk review; decompensated cirrhosis is not a routine weight-loss surgery indication. In cirrhosis, prioritize adequate protein, muscle function, and avoidance of malnutrition, with activity adapted to physical limitations. Do not apply a calorie deficit indiscriminately to a frail or malnourished patient.

check.question: An adult with obesity and MASLD has lost 4% of starting weight. Which counseling statement is most accurate?
choices: This can improve steatosis, while MASH and fibrosis outcomes require separate assessment and generally greater sustained loss.
A 4% loss proves complete fibrosis regression.
Any loss below 10% provides no liver benefit.
The percentage must be calculated using current weight as the denominator.
check.rationale: AASLD links modest 3-5% loss with steatosis improvement and generally greater than 10% loss with improvement in steatohepatitis and fibrosis. Neither a weight target nor its achievement proves an individual histologic response. Calculate percentage change from starting weight.

metadata.summary: Treat cardiovascular, kidney, diabetes, obesity, and sleep-related risk alongside fibrosis care, using evidence for the exact product and patient population.
metadata.application: Connect each medicine to its intended outcome, verify product-specific eligibility and safety, and document who will reassess cardiometabolic and liver findings.
keyPoints: MASLD alone does not justify withholding an indicated statin.
Compensated and decompensated cirrhosis require different risk assessment.
Glucose, heart failure, kidney, weight, and MASH benefits are separate claims.
Pioglitazone’s possible liver benefit does not remove its heart-failure risk.

bodies.heading: Use statins appropriately
bodies.body: Cardiovascular disease is a leading competing cause of death in MASLD. Select statin therapy and intensity according to lipid findings and ASCVD risk, with monitoring matched to the drug and clinical context. MASLD alone does not justify withholding an indicated statin; statins are generally safe in compensated cirrhosis. Decompensated cirrhosis requires greater caution, an individualized benefit-risk decision, and careful monitoring. Suspected drug-induced liver injury still needs evaluation.

bodies.heading: Separate cardiovascular and liver outcomes
bodies.body: A statin treats cardiovascular risk; it is not a treatment for MASH histology. Similarly, metformin and DPP-4 inhibitors may serve a glycemic indication but should not be selected as MASH-directed treatment on the assumption that glucose lowering proves histologic benefit. Continue appropriate comorbidity treatment while assessing liver disease separately.

bodies.heading: Choose diabetes therapy deliberately
bodies.body: For adults with type 2 diabetes, consider ASCVD, heart failure, kidney disease, weight goals, hypoglycemia risk, cost, and preferences alongside A1C. Current ADA guidance recommends agents with demonstrated cardiovascular or kidney benefits in the relevant population irrespective of A1C. SGLT2 glucose lowering declines as kidney function falls, while cardiorenal benefit can persist; check the exact product’s indication, kidney-use criteria, volume status, and safety rather than treating every product as interchangeable.

bodies.heading: Match incretin evidence to the phenotype
bodies.body: ADA recommends selected GLP-1 or dual GIP/GLP-1 therapy with demonstrated benefit for adults with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and symptomatic HFpEF, irrespective of A1C. For type 2 diabetes with MASLD and overweight or obesity, consider agents with demonstrated or potential MASH benefit as part of glycemic and weight management. Distinguish evidence, approved indication, formulation, and fibrosis stage. Wegovy injection has a specific FDA indication for adults with noncirrhotic MASH and F2-F3 fibrosis under accelerated approval based on histologic improvement, with clinical benefit subject to confirmatory verification. This does not confer a MASH indication on every incretin product or dose.

bodies.heading: Weigh pioglitazone benefit against harm
bodies.body: Pioglitazone is a PPAR-gamma agonist that improves insulin sensitivity. It can be considered for selected adults with type 2 diabetes and MASH, but its FDA indication is glycemic control in type 2 diabetes. Weight gain, edema, heart-failure exacerbation, and fracture risk affect selection. The label does not recommend use in symptomatic heart failure and contraindicates initiation in NYHA class III or IV heart failure. Assess baseline liver tests and investigate suspected injury; potential liver benefit is not a safety exemption.

bodies.heading: Reconcile other pioglitazone precautions
bodies.body: Do not use pioglitazone in active bladder cancer; a prior history calls for caution and consideration of benefit versus uncertain recurrence risk, rather than being described as the same contraindication. Review bone health and symptoms of fluid retention. Pioglitazone may restore ovulation in some premenopausal anovulatory patients, so discuss reproductive goals and unintended pregnancy risk. Check concomitant therapy and the exact label before prescribing.

bodies.heading: Treat obesity and severe hyperglycemia
bodies.body: Use sustained behavioral support and consider weight-management pharmacotherapy or metabolic surgery assessment when indicated. Insulin can promote weight gain and hypoglycemia, but may still be needed for severe or symptomatic hyperglycemia; do not withhold necessary insulin solely because MASLD or obesity is present. Individualize glucose monitoring, hypoglycemia prevention, and treatment adjustment as nutritional intake and weight change.

bodies.heading: Protect the entire system
bodies.body: Address blood pressure, lipids, smoking, kidney disease, and sleep apnea within coordinated follow-up. AASLD advises screening for sleep apnea in patients with metabolic steatotic liver disease who have overweight or obesity and considering sleep studies when risk is high. Keep indicated preventive care, reproductive goals, and access barriers in view. Assign responsibility for follow-up so liver, primary-care, diabetes, and cardiovascular plans remain connected.

check.question: An adult with MASLD and compensated cirrhosis has an established cardiovascular indication for a statin and no suspected drug-induced injury. What is the best approach?
choices: Use an appropriate statin for cardiovascular risk with monitoring matched to the drug and clinical context.
Withhold all statins because MASLD is present.
Prescribe the statin as a proven treatment for MASH histology.
Apply the same safety assessment to every patient with decompensated cirrhosis.
check.rationale: MASLD and compensated cirrhosis do not automatically preclude an indicated statin. Its purpose is cardiovascular risk reduction, not MASH histologic treatment. Decompensation requires a more cautious individualized assessment.

masld-049.question: Which weight-loss interpretation best matches AASLD’s outcome-specific guidance for an adult with overweight and MASLD?
choices: A 3-5% loss can improve steatosis; improvement in steatohepatitis and fibrosis generally requires greater sustained loss, above 10%.
A 3% loss guarantees fibrosis regression.
No liver outcome can improve until weight loss exceeds 10%.
All patients, including those with malnutrition, require the same calorie deficit.
masld-049.rationale: Modest loss is associated with steatosis improvement, while greater sustained loss is generally needed for MASH and fibrosis improvement. These are not guaranteed responses, and nutritional status affects the plan.

masld-050.question: An adult’s weight changes from 100 kg to 96 kg during MASLD care. What is the percentage loss from starting weight?
choices: 4.17%, using current weight as the denominator.
masld-050.rationale: The change is 4 kg. Divide by the 100 kg starting weight and multiply by 100: 4 / 100 × 100 = 4%. Using 96 kg changes the denominator incorrectly; 0.04 is the fraction before conversion to a percentage.

masld-051.question: A lean adult with MASLD asks whether healthy eating and activity are useful if weight loss is not needed. Which response is best?
choices: Diet quality and increased activity can benefit liver and cardiovascular health even when weight loss is not indicated.
Obesity is required before lifestyle treatment can benefit MASLD.
Every lean patient must lose more than 10% of body weight.
Exercise should begin only after ALT becomes abnormal.
masld-051.rationale: AASLD supports diet quality and activity even when weight loss is not needed. Apply weight-reduction targets to the appropriate nutritional phenotype; do not prescribe them indiscriminately or wait for an ALT rise.

masld-052.question: A patient with MASLD has clinically significant F2 fibrosis. Which alcohol recommendation is appropriate?
choices: Complete alcohol abstinence.
Continue alcohol whenever intake is below the MetALD classification threshold.
Use a normal ALT to establish that drinking is safe.
Recommend alcohol for cardiovascular protection regardless of liver fibrosis.
masld-052.rationale: AASLD recommends complete abstinence with clinically significant fibrosis, F2 or greater. SLD classification thresholds and normal enzymes are not evidence of a safe intake for this patient.

masld-053.question: A patient with MASLD becomes more active but has unchanged body weight. Which interpretation is supported?
choices: Physical activity can confer liver and cardiometabolic benefit independently of weight loss.
Activity has no possible benefit unless weight falls.
Stable weight proves fibrosis has progressed.
Activity eliminates the need for any metabolic or liver follow-up.
masld-053.rationale: Exercise can help independently of weight loss. Scale weight alone neither proves lack of benefit nor establishes fibrosis change, and continuing assessment remains necessary.

masld-054.question: A patient can safely perform five moderate aerobic sessions of 30 minutes each week. What weekly total does this provide?
choices: 150 minutes, matching a practical moderate aerobic target.
120 minutes, because the fifth session is excluded.
30 minutes, because only one session counts.
750 minutes, because both the number of sessions and weekly total are multiplied again.
masld-054.rationale: Five sessions × 30 minutes per session = 150 minutes per week. Tailor activity to ability and preferences; this arithmetic does not establish an individual histologic response.

masld-055.question: Which nutrition plan best reflects the guidance for an adult with obesity and MASLD?
choices: A sustainable calorie deficit with fiber-rich foods and unsaturated fats, reduced sugar-sweetened beverages, and culturally feasible choices.
Mandatory prolonged fasting for every patient regardless of medications and nutritional status.
Elimination of all vegetables, legumes, and whole grains because they contain carbohydrate.
A claim that one diet guarantees fibrosis regression in every patient.
masld-055.rationale: AASLD favors an appropriate calorie deficit and food quality, with fiber and unsaturated fats and reduced excess saturated fat and refined carbohydrates. Feasibility and nutrition matter; no diet guarantees a particular fibrosis response.

masld-056.question: A patient with decompensated cirrhosis, muscle loss, and poor intake is referred for weight advice. Which plan is most appropriate?
choices: Coordinate specialist nutrition and activity care that protects protein intake and muscle function; routine weight-loss surgery is inappropriate in this setting.
Apply a severe calorie deficit without assessing malnutrition.
Schedule routine bariatric surgery solely because steatosis is present.
Remove all protein to avoid liver work.
masld-056.rationale: Cirrhosis requires attention to protein, muscle function, frailty, and physical limitations. Decompensation raises major surgical risk and is not a routine metabolic-surgery indication. Indiscriminate restriction can worsen nutritional problems.

masld-057.question: Why should cardiovascular risk remain a major treatment priority in MASLD?
choices: Cardiovascular disease is a leading competing cause of death, so indicated risk-reduction care should accompany liver assessment.
Steatosis proves that cardiovascular disease cannot occur.
A normal ALT removes the need to assess blood pressure or lipids.
Fibrosis assessment substitutes for all cardiovascular prevention.
masld-057.rationale: MASLD care includes both liver-related risk and major competing cardiovascular risk. ALT or a fibrosis assessment does not replace assessment and treatment of lipids, blood pressure, glucose, and smoking.

masld-058.question: An adult with type 2 diabetes and heart failure is at their A1C goal. Which approach best reflects current guidance?
choices: Consider an SGLT2 inhibitor with demonstrated benefit for the heart-failure context, checking the exact product’s eligibility and safety irrespective of A1C.
Exclude all agents with heart-failure benefits whenever A1C is at goal.
Assume every glucose-lowering medicine has identical heart-failure outcome evidence.
Select pioglitazone solely because edema is already present.
masld-058.rationale: ADA recommends therapy with demonstrated heart-failure benefit in type 2 diabetes irrespective of A1C. Product-specific criteria and safety still apply. Glucose lowering is not proof of heart-failure benefit, and pioglitazone can exacerbate fluid retention and heart failure.

masld-059.question: An adult with type 2 diabetes and MASH also has symptomatic NYHA class III heart failure. Which pioglitazone interpretation is correct?
choices: Initiating pioglitazone is contraindicated; possible liver benefit does not override the heart-failure restriction.
MASH removes the labeled heart-failure contraindication.
Pioglitazone treats fluid retention and should be started to reduce edema.
All medicines discussed for MASH have identical cardiac safety.
masld-059.rationale: The pioglitazone label contraindicates initiation in NYHA class III or IV heart failure and does not recommend use in symptomatic heart failure. Its potential benefit in selected patients with diabetes and MASH must be weighed against weight gain, edema, and heart-failure risk.

masld-060.question: An adult with obesity and MASLD has severe symptomatic hyperglycemia requiring insulin consideration. Which reasoning is most appropriate?
choices: Assess and treat the severe hyperglycemia, including insulin when needed, while planning weight and hypoglycemia management.
Withhold insulin solely because it can cause weight gain.
Wait for ALT to rise before treating hyperglycemia.
Assume MASLD prevents all hypoglycemia during insulin treatment.
masld-060.rationale: Insulin may be necessary for severe or symptomatic hyperglycemia. Weight gain and hypoglycemia risks require a plan, but do not justify withholding necessary treatment solely because obesity or MASLD is present.

masld-061.question: An adult with MASLD and compensated cirrhosis has an established ASCVD indication for a statin, with no suspected drug-induced liver injury. Which plan is best?
choices: Select an appropriate statin for cardiovascular risk and monitor in the drug and clinical context.
Withhold every statin because hepatic steatosis is present.
Use the statin as a proven therapy for MASH histology.
Wait for hepatic decompensation before addressing ASCVD.
masld-061.rationale: An indicated statin should not be withheld solely because MASLD or compensated cirrhosis is present. Statins reduce cardiovascular risk; they are not MASH-directed histologic treatment. Decompensation warrants greater caution, not delayed cardiovascular assessment.

masld-062.question: Which distinction is most accurate when considering a statin in decompensated cirrhosis?
choices: Safety data are more limited and adverse-event risk may be higher, requiring an individualized benefit-risk assessment and careful monitoring.
Decompensation has exactly the same evidence and risk profile as compensated cirrhosis.
Any cardiovascular benefit proves that the statin reverses MASH fibrosis.
A single normal ALT eliminates the need for a clinical safety assessment.
masld-062.rationale: AASLD describes more limited evidence and greater caution in decompensated cirrhosis. Selected patients with high cardiovascular risk may still be considered for treatment with careful monitoring, rather than applying a blanket rule from compensated disease.

masld-063.question: Which conclusion about diabetes medicines and MASH is justified?
choices: Match the exact product, formulation, indication, and patient population; glycemic efficacy alone does not establish MASH histologic benefit.
Every GLP-1 product and dose has the same FDA MASH indication.
Metformin’s glucose lowering proves it treats MASH histology.
A DPP-4 inhibitor’s renal dose adjustment proves antifibrotic efficacy.
masld-063.rationale: Glucose, weight, cardiovascular, kidney, and MASH outcomes must be distinguished. Specific Wegovy injection approval does not extend to every incretin product or dose. Metformin and DPP-4 inhibitors should not be selected as MASH-directed therapy on the basis of glucose lowering alone.

masld-064.question: Which safety interpretation of pioglitazone matches its label?
choices: Avoid use in active bladder cancer; a prior history requires caution and assessment of benefit versus uncertain recurrence risk.
Active bladder cancer is irrelevant whenever the patient has MASH.
A prior history and active bladder cancer are described as identical restrictions in the current label.
Possible MASH benefit removes the need to consider fractures or fluid retention.
masld-064.rationale: The label distinguishes active bladder cancer, where pioglitazone should not be used, from a prior history requiring caution and benefit-risk review. Fractures, fluid retention, weight gain, and heart-failure risk remain relevant.

noninsulin-diabetes-06-application.question: An adult with type 2 diabetes and CKD has reduced glucose lowering from an SGLT2 inhibitor as kidney function falls. Which interpretation is best?
choices: Reduced glucose lowering does not necessarily eliminate cardiorenal benefit; reassess the exact product’s indication, kidney-use criteria, volume status, and safety.
Every decline in glucose lowering proves that all cardiorenal benefit has disappeared.
Kidney function and volume status are irrelevant to every SGLT2 prescription.
All SGLT2 products have identical indications at every level of kidney function.
noninsulin-diabetes-06-application.rationale: SGLT2 glucose-lowering efficacy declines with reduced kidney function, while benefits for selected cardiovascular and kidney outcomes can persist in studied populations. Check the chosen product and clinical context rather than equating glycemic response with every outcome.

noninsulin-diabetes-12-application.question: Which DPP-4 inhibitor kidney-use distinction is correct?
choices: Sitagliptin, saxagliptin, and alogliptin require kidney-based dose adjustment; linagliptin does not require a renal dose adjustment.
Linagliptin always requires the same renal adjustment as sitagliptin.
Every DPP-4 inhibitor has identical renal elimination and adjustment rules.
Renal dose adjustment establishes that the drug is a proven MASH histologic treatment.
noninsulin-diabetes-12-application.rationale: The supplied book differentiates the renal adjustment requirements, and the linagliptin label confirms no renal dosage adjustment. Linagliptin is primarily eliminated through nonrenal pathways. These pharmacokinetic distinctions do not establish a MASH treatment indication.

noninsulin-diabetes-18-application.question: An alert patient who can swallow develops mild hypoglycemia while using acarbose with a sulfonylurea. Which oral carbohydrate is appropriate for rapid treatment?
choices: Glucose (dextrose).
Sucrose, because acarbose accelerates its breakdown.
Acarbose itself, because it raises glucose directly.
No carbohydrate, because acarbose makes sulfonylurea-associated hypoglycemia impossible.
noninsulin-diabetes-18-application.rationale: Acarbose does not usually cause hypoglycemia alone, but concomitant insulin or a secretagogue can. Glucose is directly absorbable; sucrose requires hydrolysis that acarbose delays and is unsuitable for rapid correction. Severe hypoglycemia requires a different rescue approach.

noninsulin-diabetes-24-application.question: An adult with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and symptomatic HFpEF is at their A1C goal. Which treatment reasoning best reflects current ADA guidance?
choices: Consider a GLP-1 or dual GIP/GLP-1 agent with demonstrated benefit for the specific HFpEF population, irrespective of A1C, while checking product-specific eligibility and tolerability.
Exclude all incretin therapy solely because A1C is at goal.
Assume every incretin product has identical HFpEF evidence and FDA indications.
Choose a DPP-4 inhibitor’s renal dose solely as proof of improved HFpEF symptoms.
noninsulin-diabetes-24-application.rationale: ADA 2026 recommendations distinguish selected GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 therapies with demonstrated benefits for adults with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and symptomatic HFpEF. A1C does not replace the relevant outcome indication; exact product and population evidence, safety, and tolerability matter.

bodies.heading: Use statins appropriately
bodies.body: Cardiovascular disease is a leading competing cause of death in MASLD. Select statin therapy and intensity according to lipid findings and ASCVD risk, with monitoring matched to the drug and clinical context. MASLD alone does not justify withholding an indicated statin; statins are generally safe in compensated cirrhosis. Decompensated cirrhosis requires greater caution, an individualized benefit-risk decision, and careful monitoring. Suspected drug-induced liver injury still needs evaluation.

bodies.heading: Separate cardiovascular and liver outcomes
bodies.body: A statin treats cardiovascular risk; it is not a treatment for MASH histology. Similarly, metformin and DPP-4 inhibitors may serve a glycemic indication but should not be selected as MASH-directed treatment on the assumption that glucose lowering proves histologic benefit. Continue appropriate comorbidity treatment while assessing liver disease separately.

bodies.heading: Choose diabetes therapy deliberately
bodies.body: For adults with type 2 diabetes, consider ASCVD, heart failure, kidney disease, weight goals, hypoglycemia risk, cost, and preferences alongside A1C. Current ADA guidance recommends agents with demonstrated cardiovascular or kidney benefits in the relevant population irrespective of A1C. SGLT2 glucose lowering declines as kidney function falls, while cardiorenal benefit can persist; check the exact product’s indication, kidney-use criteria, volume status, and safety rather than treating every product as interchangeable.

bodies.heading: Match incretin evidence to the phenotype
bodies.body: ADA recommends selected GLP-1 or dual GIP/GLP-1 therapy with demonstrated benefit for adults with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and symptomatic HFpEF, irrespective of A1C. For type 2 diabetes with MASLD and overweight or obesity, consider agents with demonstrated or potential MASH benefit as part of glycemic and weight management. Distinguish evidence, approved indication, formulation, and fibrosis stage. Wegovy injection has a specific FDA indication for adults with noncirrhotic MASH and F2-F3 fibrosis under accelerated approval based on histologic improvement, with clinical benefit subject to confirmatory verification. This does not confer a MASH indication on every incretin product or dose.

bodies.heading: Weigh pioglitazone benefit against harm
bodies.body: Pioglitazone is a PPAR-gamma agonist that improves insulin sensitivity. It can be considered for selected adults with type 2 diabetes and MASH, but its FDA indication is glycemic control in type 2 diabetes. Weight gain, edema, heart-failure exacerbation, and fracture risk affect selection. The label does not recommend use in symptomatic heart failure and contraindicates initiation in NYHA class III or IV heart failure. Assess baseline liver tests and investigate suspected injury; potential liver benefit is not a safety exemption.

bodies.heading: Reconcile other pioglitazone precautions
bodies.body: Do not use pioglitazone in active bladder cancer; a prior history calls for caution and consideration of benefit versus uncertain recurrence risk, rather than being described as the same contraindication. Review bone health and symptoms of fluid retention. Pioglitazone may restore ovulation in some premenopausal anovulatory patients, so discuss reproductive goals and unintended pregnancy risk. Check concomitant therapy and the exact label before prescribing.

bodies.heading: Treat obesity and severe hyperglycemia
bodies.body: Use sustained behavioral support and consider weight-management pharmacotherapy or metabolic surgery assessment when indicated. Insulin can promote weight gain and hypoglycemia, but may still be needed for severe or symptomatic hyperglycemia; do not withhold necessary insulin solely because MASLD or obesity is present. Individualize glucose monitoring, hypoglycemia prevention, and treatment adjustment as nutritional intake and weight change.

bodies.heading: Protect the entire system
bodies.body: Address blood pressure, lipids, smoking, kidney disease, and sleep apnea within coordinated follow-up. AASLD advises screening for sleep apnea in patients with metabolic steatotic liver disease who have overweight or obesity and considering sleep studies when risk is high. Keep indicated preventive care, reproductive goals, and access barriers in view. Assign responsibility for follow-up so liver, primary-care, diabetes, and cardiovascular plans remain connected.

check.question: An adult with MASLD and compensated cirrhosis has an established cardiovascular indication for a statin and no suspected drug-induced injury. What is the best approach?
choices: Use an appropriate statin for cardiovascular risk with monitoring matched to the drug and clinical context.
Withhold all statins because MASLD is present.
Prescribe the statin as a proven treatment for MASH histology.
Apply the same safety assessment to every patient with decompensated cirrhosis.
check.rationale: MASLD and compensated cirrhosis do not automatically preclude an indicated statin. Its purpose is cardiovascular risk reduction, not MASH histologic treatment. Decompensation requires a more cautious individualized assessment.

wholeItemReviewed.question: An alert patient who can swallow develops mild hypoglycemia while using acarbose with a sulfonylurea. Which oral carbohydrate is appropriate for rapid treatment?
choices: Glucose (dextrose).
Sucrose, because acarbose accelerates its breakdown.
Acarbose itself, because it raises glucose directly.
No carbohydrate, because acarbose makes sulfonylurea-associated hypoglycemia impossible.
wholeItemReviewed.rationale: Acarbose does not usually cause hypoglycemia alone, but concomitant insulin or a secretagogue can. Glucose is directly absorbable; sucrose requires hydrolysis that acarbose delays and is unsuitable for rapid correction. Severe hypoglycemia requires a different rescue approach.

wholeItemReviewed.question: An adult with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and symptomatic HFpEF is at their A1C goal. Which treatment reasoning best reflects current ADA guidance?
choices: Consider a GLP-1 or dual GIP/GLP-1 agent with demonstrated benefit for the specific HFpEF population, irrespective of A1C, while checking product-specific eligibility and tolerability.
Exclude all incretin therapy solely because A1C is at goal.
Assume every incretin product has identical HFpEF evidence and FDA indications.
Choose a DPP-4 inhibitor’s renal dose solely as proof of improved HFpEF symptoms.
wholeItemReviewed.rationale: ADA 2026 recommendations distinguish selected GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 therapies with demonstrated benefits for adults with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and symptomatic HFpEF. A1C does not replace the relevant outcome indication; exact product and population evidence, safety, and tolerability matter.
